1: The Gospel is God's power to save

Paul greets the Christians of Rome and says he is not ashamed of the Gospel. He then shows the Gentile world's problem: people could know God from what he has made, but they chose idols, and their lives fell apart as a result.
God can be known by reason from creation. Turning from him is the root of moral disorder.
2: Paul turns to those who condemn others while doing the same things. God will repay each person according to their works and has no favourites. Gentiles have the law written on their hearts in conscience; having the Law of Moses does not help unless it is kept.
Everyone has a conscience that points to right and wrong. Religious privilege is no shield against judgement.
3: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin; no one is righteous by their own record. But now God offers righteousness as a gift, through faith in Jesus Christ, whose blood makes up for sins.
Nobody earns salvation. It is a gift won by Christ's sacrifice, and it leaves no room for boasting.
4: Abraham was counted righteous because he trusted God's promise, before he was circumcised. So he is the father of everyone who believes, Jew or Gentile. He believed that God could give life to the dead.
Faith was always the way to God, even in the Old Testament. Abraham's trust is the pattern for ours.
5: Peace with God; Adam and Christ

Made right with God through faith, we have peace and a hope that does not disappoint, because God's love has been poured into our hearts. Through one man, Adam, sin and death came into the world. Through one man, Christ, grace and life overflow.
This chapter is a key source for the teaching on original sin. Christ's gift is far greater than Adam's damage.
6: Dead to sin, alive in Christ
Should we sin more so that grace increases? Never. In baptism we were buried with Christ and raised to a new life. We are no longer slaves of sin, and we should offer ourselves to God.
Baptism really changes us; it is not only a symbol. Grace is the power to stop sinning, not permission to carry on.
7: Paul says the Law is good, but it shows up sin without giving the power to defeat it. He describes the experience of wanting to do good and doing the evil he hates. "Who will rescue me? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ."
Everyone knows this inner battle. Knowing what is right is not enough; we need grace.
8: There is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. The Spirit makes us God's children, who can call him "Abba, Father". Creation groans, waiting to be set free, and the Spirit helps us pray. Nothing can separate us from the love of God.
This is one of the greatest chapters in the Bible. God works all things for good for those who love him.
9: Paul grieves that most of his own people have not accepted Christ. He explains that God's promise has not failed: God has always been free in choosing, as with Isaac and Jacob, and he shows mercy as he wills.
Salvation depends on God's mercy, not on ancestry or effort. Paul treats this as a mystery to adore, not a puzzle to solve.
10: Israel was zealous for God but tried to set up its own righteousness. Salvation is near: confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him. But people cannot believe unless someone is sent to preach.
This is why the Church sends missionaries. Faith is a response to a message someone has to bring.
11: God has not rejected Israel. Some natural branches were broken off and Gentiles, like wild shoots, were grafted in, so they must not be proud. In the end all Israel will be saved. Paul ends in praise of God's wisdom.
Christians owe respect and gratitude to the Jewish people. God's gifts and his call are never withdrawn.
12: Because of God's mercy, offer your whole self to him and do not be shaped by the world. The Church is one body with different gifts. Love sincerely, bless those who persecute you, and overcome evil with good.
Here doctrine turns into daily life. Worship includes how we live from Monday to Saturday.
13: Paul teaches respect for lawful authority and paying what is owed. The one lasting debt is to love one another, which fulfils the whole law. The night is nearly over, so put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
Christians are good citizens. It was verses 13 and 14 that Augustine read at the moment of his conversion.
14: Christians disagreed about food and special days. Paul says not to despise or judge one another over such matters, since each will answer to God. Do not let your freedom make a weaker believer stumble.
On things that are not essential, charity matters more than being right.
15: The strong should carry the weaknesses of the weak, following Christ, who did not please himself. Christ came for both Jews and Gentiles. Paul describes his mission and his plan to visit Rome on the way to Spain.
The Scriptures were written to give us hope. Unity in the Church is built by patience.
16: Paul commends Phoebe, who carries the letter, and greets a long list of co-workers by name, many of them women. He warns against those who cause divisions and ends with praise to God.
The early Church was a network of real friendships. Paul remembers people one by one.
